questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val a = Point(1, 2)
    val b = Point(1, 2)
    println(a == b)
    println(a === b)
}
questions.explanation: `==` is structural equality and calls the generated `equals`, which compares `x` and `y`. `===` is referential equality, and `a` and `b` are two separate objects, so it is `false`.

questions.question: In Kotlin, what does `a == b` compile to when `a` and `b` are nullable references?
questions.explanation: `==` is null-safe: if `a` is non-null it calls `a.equals(b)`, otherwise it is true only when `b` is also null. It never throws a NullPointerException, unlike calling `equals` directly in Java.

questions.question: Given `var name = "ada"`, calling `name.uppercase()` on its own line changes `name` to `"ADA"`.
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable. `uppercase()` returns a new String and leaves `name` unchanged. You must assign the result, e.g. `name = name.uppercase()`.

questions.question: A Retrofit model is declared as a plain `class`, not a `data class`. Two responses produce objects with identical fields. What does `old == new` return?
questions.code:
class UserDto(val id: Int, val name: String)

val old = UserDto(1, "Ada")
val new = UserDto(1, "Ada")
val same = old == new
options: `true`, because `==` compares field by field using reflection
It does not compile, because `==` needs a data class
questions.explanation: A regular class inherits `equals` from `Any`, which is identity-based. Only a `data class` (or a manual `equals` override) compares property values.

questions.question: Why is `buildString { for (line in lines) append(line) }` preferred over `var s = ""; for (line in lines) s += line` for large lists?
options: Each `+=` allocates a new String; `buildString` appends to one `StringBuilder`
`+=` on a String does not compile inside a loop
`buildString` runs the loop on a background thread, so the main thread isn't blocked
`+=` silently drops characters once the String passes 64 KB on Android
questions.explanation: Because String is immutable, each `+=` copies the whole accumulated text into a new object, which makes the loop quadratic. `buildString` gives you a mutable `StringBuilder` and calls `toString()` once at the end.

questions.question: `Nothing` has no instances, so a function whose return type is `Nothing` can never return normally. It can only throw or loop forever.
questions.explanation: No value of type `Nothing` exists, so such a function can never produce one to return. That is why `throw` expressions and `error()` have type `Nothing`, and why code after them is unreachable.

questions.question: Why does `fun loadUser(): User = TODO()` compile even though `TODO()` builds no `User`?
options: `TODO()` returns `Nothing`, which is a subtype of every type
`TODO()` returns `Any`, which is cast to `User` automatically
`TODO()` returns `null`, and the compiler makes the return type `User?`
The compiler skips type checking for any function that calls `TODO()`
questions.explanation: `TODO()` is an ordinary stdlib function declared to return `Nothing`, which is a subtype of every type. It type-checks anywhere and throws `NotImplementedError` when called. It does not return `null` or `Any`.

questions.question: Which expressions evaluate to the string `"07"`?
questions.explanation: `padStart` adds the padding on the left, giving `"07"`, and reversing `"70"` also gives `"07"`. `padEnd` pads on the right (`"70"`), and `substring(1, 2)` excludes the end index, so it returns only `"0"`.

questions.question: `UiState` is a data class. The ViewModel assigns a new instance whose properties equal the current value. What do the collectors of `state` receive?
options: Nothing, because StateFlow skips a value `==` to the current one
The new value, because it is a different object (`!==`)
The new value twice, once for each changed property
An exception, because StateFlow values must be immutable singletons
questions.explanation: StateFlow conflates by equality: when the new value `equals` the current one, it does not emit. With a data class that is structural equality, so an identical `UiState` causes no recomposition or re-render.

questions.question: In a `DiffUtil.ItemCallback<Item>` where `Item` is a data class, `areContentsTheSame = oldItem == newItem` will NOT notice a change to a `var` declared in the class body instead of the primary constructor.
questions.explanation: Data class `equals` compares only primary-constructor properties. A change to a body property leaves the items equal, so DiffUtil decides nothing changed and the row is never rebound.

questions.question: What does this print on the JVM? (The compiler warns about `===` on `Int?`, but it compiles.)
questions.code:
fun main() {
    val a: Int? = 127
    val b: Int? = 127
    val c: Int? = 128
    val d: Int? = 128
    println(a === b)
    println(c === d)
    println(c == d)
}
questions.explanation: `Int?` is boxed as `java.lang.Integer`, and `Integer.valueOf` caches values from -128 to 127, so both 127s are the same object while the two 128s are different boxes. `==` compares values, so `c == d` is still `true`.

questions.question: Which statements are true?
options: `Any` is the root of the non-nullable type hierarchy
`Unit` is an object with exactly one value
`Unit` has no instances, just like Java `void`
The only value of type `Nothing?` is `null`
A function declared as `fun log() {}` returns `Nothing`
questions.explanation: `Unit` is a real singleton object, which is why `val u = println()` works. `Nothing` is the type with no instances, so `Nothing?` can hold only `null`. A block-bodied function with no return type returns `Unit`, not `Nothing`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
fun main() {
    val x = Double.NaN
    val y: Any = Double.NaN
    println(x == x)
    println(y == y)
    println(x < 1.0 || x >= 1.0)
}
questions.explanation: When the static type is `Double`, `==` follows IEEE 754, where `NaN` is not equal to itself and every comparison with it is false. When the static type is `Any`, `==` calls `Double.equals`, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself.

questions.question: What is `"a,,b,".split(",").size` in Kotlin?
questions.explanation: Kotlin's `split` keeps every empty piece, giving `["a", "", "b", ""]`. Java's `String.split` drops trailing empty strings and would give 3, which is the common trap.
